In the invitation to make this presentation by the meeting organizers, we were asked to include a discussion of peptide directed imaging and theranostics to areas that would be of interest to the attendees, which primarily includes studies related to the CNS. The interest in the possible application of peptide theranostics to oncology both generally and in the case of the CNS tumors has markedly increased over the last few years because of its successful application in both neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer, leading to FDA approved novel tumor approaches for both imaging these tumors as well as for its theranostic approach. In this paper we review the scientific basis for the successful application of peptide theranostics to neuroendocrine and prostate cancer, and the current status of its application to CNS tumors, particularly meningiomas, glioblastomas including glioblastoma multiforme, and medulloblastomas. We particularly concentrate on the possible use of the somatostatin, bombesin (Bn), and substance P (SP)/neurokinin (NK) family of receptors as targets, which have received the most attention and show the most promise in applying peptide receptor imaging/theranostics to CNS tumors. We also discuss the specific problems that the CNS presents in applying this approach to CNS tumors because of the blood-brain barrier in addition to the progress made. Clinical Trial Registry: NCT01578239 (NETTER-1)(NET), NCT03972488 (NETTER-2)(NET): VISION Trial (NCT03511664)[Lu-177-PSMA-617] (Pluvicto) in advanced prostate cancer.

42858234.title: Fanconi anemia pathway disruption drives lomustine sensitivity in glioma.
42858234.abstract: Therapeutic options for progressive glioblastoma remain limited, with chlorethyl-cyclohexyl-nitrosourea (CCNU, lomustine) among the approved treatments. Beyond MGMT gene promoter methylation, molecular determinants of CCNU sensitivity or resistance are ill- defined. We employed genome-wide functional knockout screening using the CRISPR-Cas9 technology to identify and subsequently validate modulators of response to CCNU in experimental glioma. We established an immunocompetent glioma mouse model to enable functional interrogation of Fanconi anemia pathway (FA) genes in tumor growth and synthetic lethal interactions in vivo using the RCAS/tv-a somatic gene delivery system. Multiple FA pathway members recurrently emerged as potent synthetic lethal interactors of CCNU treatment. In vivo knockdown of Fancm accelerated tumor onset and significantly increased CCNU sensitivity. Consistently, FA pathway inhibition enhanced CCNU efficacy across in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo models. Together, these findings identify FA pathway components as key synthetic lethal interactors of CCNU response and reveal a therapeutically actionable vulnerability in glioblastoma. Treatment options for glioblastoma are very limited. This study examined molecular modulators of treatment sensitivity regarding the approved drug lomustine. Using a functional genomic screening approach and different cell-based and in vivo models, this study discoverd that glioblastomas with reduced activity in a group of genes responsible for repairing damaged DNA are more sensitive to lomustine. Lowering the activity of one key gene, called FancM, strongly improved the effect of lomustine. These results might inform strategies to patient stratification for lomustine treatment in the short run while enabling novel combination therapies in the long term.

42865025.title: A Multi-Omic Phenobank Reveals Axes of Glioblastoma Growth, Invasion, and Therapeutic Vulnerability.
42865025.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) invasion is clinically decisive but difficult to model systematically. Existing patient-derived xenograft (PDX) resources rarely couple reproducible in vivo invasion phenotypes with matched multi-omic profiles at scale, limiting mechanistic insight and phenotype-informed therapeutic hypotheses. We established the HGCC Phenobank, comprising 65 patient-derived GBM stem-like cultures with matched multi-omic profiling and orthotopic engraftment in 449 mice. Blinded histopathology quantified ten invasion traits per case. These phenotypes were integrated with RNA sequencing, DNA methylation, and mass-spectrometry-based proteomics. Multi-Omic Factor Analysis (MOFA) identified latent molecular programs. Phenotype-specific RNA signatures were matched to LINCS drug-perturbation profiles and validated in 3D gliomasphere and ex vivo brain-slice assays. Two dominant, reproducible invasion modes emerged across models: diffuse parenchymal infiltration and perivascular/condensed growth. Proneural cultures formed more aggressive tumors in immunodeficient mice, and mouse survival showed a modest correlation with patient survival in matched cases (Pearson r=0.1832, p=0.045). MOFA identified 15 latent factors; Factor 1, marked by ASCL1/OLIG1/OLIG2 programs across multiple molecular layers, was associated with increased tumor formation and diffuse invasion in mice. Higher Factor 1 scores were associated with significantly longer postoperative survival in both the matched patient cohort (p = 0.00018) and TCGA (p = 0.017), although Factor 1 was not associated with survival of the xenografted mice. Drug-signature matching separated mechanisms targeting diffuse versus perivascular invasion. Experimental validation confirmed phenotype-selective sensitivities, and inhibitors PIK-75 and buparlisib suppressed invasion dynamics across representative models in 3D and brain-slice assays. The HGCC Phenobank provides the first openly available PDX resource that systematically links GBM invasion phenotypes to multi-omic programs and therapeutic predictions. This framework enables reproducible model selection, mechanistic dissection of invasion modes, and phenotype-guided therapeutic discovery. Glioblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer. Its spread into surrounding tissue makes surgical removal impossible and contributes to short patient survival. We built 65 patient-derived tumor cell models and grew them as tumors in mice, measuring how each model grows and invades. Combining these observations with genetic and molecular data, we identified two distinct invasion patterns — diffuse spread through brain tissue and growth along blood vessels — each driven by different molecular programs. We used these profiles to predict and validate drugs that selectively slow invasion, offering a new framework for targeted glioblastoma treatment.

42895284.title: Biomarker-guided treatment strategies for patients with gliomas in clinical practice.
42895284.abstract: Targeted therapy has made important contributions to improving outcomes for patients with many solid tumors, but has had only limited activity so far in patients with gliomas, notably glioblastoma. Failure of targeted therapy in glioblastoma is likely due to redundance of oncogenic pathway activation and so far the inability to identify suitable targets and apply biomarker-based enrichment strategies in clinical trial designs. In contrast, in non-glioblastoma tumors, there are promising developments which have already changed clinical practice: inhibition of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) exemplified by vorasidenib, the first approved drug specifically for IDH-mutant gliomas, has changed the landscape for targeted therapy of WHO grade 2 gliomas. Furthermore, dordaviprone, an antagonist of dopamine receptor D2/3 (DRD2/3) and an allosteric agonist of the mitochondrial protease caseinolytic mitochondrial matrix peptidase proteolytic subunit (ClpP), emerges as a potentially active agent in patients with recurrent K27M-mutant diffuse midline gliomas. Finally, BRAF mutations, neurotrophic tyrosine receptor kinase ( r fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) gene fusions continue to raise interest as therapeutic targets at least for subsets of patients with gliomas. Almost no targeted therapy approaches for ependymomas have emerged. Improved clinical trial designs including shared control arms early on and using pharmacodynamic endpoints ideally in enriched patient populations are the path forward towards the identification of further active treatments for patients with gliomas. Targeted therapy defines treatment strategies that are designed to interfere with a specific metabolic signaling pathway that maintains growth of a specific type of tumor. Among primary brain tumors, dependence of growth on one single signaling pathway is rare. This has limited the role of targeted therapy, notably in glioblastoma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults. In some brain tumors other than glioblastoma, there are promising developments which have already changed clinical practice, notably inhibition of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) in tumors with IDH mutations. Novel targets are currently being explored in various types of rare brain tumors.

42895289.title: Novel therapies for glioblastoma.
42895289.abstract: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive and treatment-resistant primary brain tumor in adults. Given its clinical severity and biological complexity, research efforts are focused on understanding and targeting intratumoral heterogeneity, adaptive resistance, drug delivery barriers, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. This review highlights emerging therapeutic approaches for the treatment of glioblastoma including advances in radiation planning, molecularly targeted therapy, immunotherapy, blood-brain barrier modulation, and neuronal signaling. Radiation therapy remains a cornerstone of glioblastoma treatment, and advances in image-guided planning are being developed to refine treatment margins and improve tolerability without compromising efficacy. Blood-brain barrier permeability is being improved through device-assisted approaches, including focused ultrasound in combination with systemic therapies. Molecularly targeted and immunotherapeutic approaches continue to be evaluated, increasingly with biomarker-informed strategies to optimize patient selection. In parallel, drug repurposing, neuronal modulation, and metabolic interventions have shown promising preclinical and retrospective signals and are moving towards prospective studies. Interventions to improve quality of life are also underway with early palliative care showing significant impact for patients with glioblastoma. As the field moves towards tailored and precision-guided approaches, combination strategies remain central to addressing the multiple mechanisms by which glioblastoma evades treatment.

42911751.title: Development of DCL1191 as a Potent, Selective and Orally Bioavailable Inhibitor for Autophagy-Associated Transcription Factor EB (TFEB).
42911751.abstract: Transcription factor EB (TFEB) is a promising target for autophagy regulation and cancer therapy, yet it has long been regarded as an undruggable protein. Starting from eltrombopag, an FDA-approved agent that exhibits both thrombopoietin receptor (Tpo-R) agonistic activity and TFEB inhibitory potency, we performed systematic structure-activity relationship optimization and identified DCL1191 as a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable TFEB inhibitor. DCL1191 binds TFEB with a Kd of 80.5 nM and disrupts the TFEB-DNA interaction with an IC50 of 60.5 nM. Computational modeling combined with site-directed mutagenesis elucidated its precise binding mode. DCL1191 exhibits diminished activity toward Tpo-R and MITF. Mechanistically, DCL1191 effectively represses the transcription of TFEB target genes and blocks intracellular autophagic flux. In autophagy-hyperactivated U87 glioblastoma cells, DCL1191 substantially sensitizes tumor cells to temozolomide chemotherapy. Pharmacokinetic evaluation in rats further demonstrated that DCL1191 possesses an i.v. half-life of 16.33 h and satisfactory oral bioavailability of 18.77%.

42936488.title: Functional divergence of the synapsin family in glioblastoma: Synapsin III as a candidate differentiation-restoring node.
42936488.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains an aggressive adult primary brain tumor despite surgery, radiotherapy and temozolomide-based chemotherapy, partly because glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) retain self-renewal capacity, lineage plasticity and therapeutic resistance. Cancer neuroscience has shown that glioma cells receive activity-dependent neuronal signals and exploit neural circuits to support tumor growth and invasion. Synaptic proteins may therefore regulate both neuron-glioma communication and tumor-cell state. Synapsin I, II, and III share conserved N-terminal domains but differ in C-terminal architecture, developmental expression and physiological function. An emerging model of functional divergence in GBM is supported by a recent preclinical study comparing Synapsin III with Synapsin I and II. In the tested GSC models, increasing Synapsin III promoted a neuronal-like differentiated phenotype through a neuregulin 3 (NRG3)-JAG1-NOTCH1 mechanism, with reduced stemness and proliferative growth. This review integrates structural, physiological and GBM-focused evidence to examine how the developmental functions of Synapsin III may be repurposed in malignant stem-like cells. Independent replication, durable loss of tumorigenicity and tumor-selective delivery are priorities for translation. Synapsin III is a candidate differentiation-restoring node whose clinical relevance remains to be established.
